Phainon closed his eyes. “‘Dei, can we not discuss it over the phone? Let’s talk about it when I’m back, okay? I’ll be in Okhema in six hours. I…”

… I want to do this right. I want to see you. I want you to know that I’m fine. I could keep up with your world. I could rise to your sky, too. But I can’t do it here in a city I am not familiar with. I’d rather we do it in the safety of our sanctuary, where we’re invincible and no one could touch us. Please, please…

He couldn’t say that out loud, not after his betrayal.

“... Please.”

There was a sharp inhale, another pause, and a flicker of unspoken heartbreak that Phainon could feel filling in the silence. He could feel his chest burn. His shoulders were heavy with the weight of his own lies.

“I can’t be home until Monday,” Mydei said. “I’m in Epsilon. There’s a typhoon forecasted tonight.”

Epsilon. Eight-hour flight, not including the delays that could possibly happen in typhoon season. The Southern Hemisphere was always weird. Phainon would know. He got weather reports of it every now and then.

“I’ll… be back on Wednesday,” Phainon said. “I’ve got a short regional on Monday afternoon. I’ll be back Wednesday morning.”

There was another sharp, defeated intake of breath. “Fine,” he said. “But if you’re ready to talk before then, call me. Alright? If I don’t pick up, call Krateros. If he doesn’t pick up, call Hephaestion. He’s always on his phone. Please do that, Phainon. Please. Talk to me.”

“Okay,” Phainon said. “I promise.”

Mydei hummed, and Phainon could see the scoff underneath that.

What good was a promise now? He’d already lied. What’s another?

“Alright,” Mydei said. “See you then.”

“See you, ‘Dei. I love you.”

The sweet words he said with his whole heart tasted the same as the lie he just told Mydei.

“Love you, HKS.”

There was another stretch of silence from Mydei’s side, like he was waiting for something. But then, exactly five seconds later, he hung up the phone.

Phainon wondered what that was about until he remembered it.

The kisses.

Phainon always demands kisses before they part. Now, he was so fucked up he even forgot that.

Phainon placed his phone back on the table, staring at the unanswered messages, and realized how easily he lied. How easily he offered something that he dreaded, so that he could put off that uncomfortable feeling of having to talk about it.

As he cleaned up his plate, went back to his room, and saw his flight plan for Okhema City, he felt even more hollow.

Although he was flying home base, he felt he was drifting further away from home.

-

Phainon had tried to follow Dan Heng’s advice to stay off the grid and avoid the news about Mydei.

He tried.

Still, even though he had his phone sat deep in his pocket, even though he actively did not look at the news or social media during his journey to and from the airport, Phainon couldn’t seem to escape the #LionDove.

It was everywhere.

Phainon could even piece together what happened during the rest of the talk show just from overhearing about it here and there. Mydei and Rob sang Goddess live. Mydei got so flustered that he avoided Rob’s eyes. Mydei stared at her like she was a goddess. They’re such a couple goal. Rob’s so in love. Rob’s so lucky to have Mydei.

Rob completed Mydei perfectly. They’re truly a couple of royalty.

And as he glanced at the TV, watching their duet on repeat, he couldn’t even argue with it.

They looked so great together.

Their chemistry was so great that they could even revive the spirit of Queen Gorgo.

Together, there was nothing that they couldn’t do.

Those words echoed in every corner of what little world Phainon passed by between his flight and his home. Their presence was so massive that by the time Phainon was finally back at their apartment, Mydei’s absence was so palpable.

And without him, the house felt too large, too empty, matching too perfectly with the hollow that sat deep inside Phainon’s chest.

This felt like a place of abandon, with Mydei’s spices, cooking utensils, his boxes of meal prep in the refrigerator, the painting he bought at a charity auction, his perfume, his boxes of sponsored shoes…

This was Mydei’s home. The evidence of his presence was everywhere, and yet, this house was so void of him.

Phainon sat on the kitchen’s stool, staring at Mydei’s last chat. He had stopped pestering him about the talk show, only messaging Phainon about his schedule and his day, hinting at it in a short message: "Tell me if you’re ready."

Phainon had replied with 'Wednesday, okay?'

And that was another lie.

Because Phainon had just received approval to switch his short regional week for an ultra-long-haul flight, which meant flying two 16-hour legs and spending three days on a layover.

He wouldn’t be back to Okhema until next Wednesday.

Technically, it wasn’t a lie.

He’d still see Mydei on Wednesday. Only a week apart from what he promised.

It felt like a foul play, like another lie. But Phainon really couldn’t face Mydei when the burning shame was still eating his heart. He closed his phone, and as the night crawled deeper, Phainon could no longer stand the quiet of their apartment.

The isolation of not being able to talk about his worries with his friends, the alienation of not even being able to access his phone in the risk of Mydei - Robin exposure, the looming guilt of lying to Mydei, the burning shame of getting caught, the crushing weight of seeing Mydei anywhere but here in their sanctuary…

No.

He couldn’t do this.

Phainon packed his suitcase and decided to book the cheapest flight he could find. He didn’t care where it went. He wouldn’t even board the plane. He just wanted to get a boarding pass to use his perk on the VIP lounge— the only place he could think of getting rest without having to bear the quiet of the empty room. At least there, there would be strangers, noise, and fluorescent lights.

If he had to sleep on another recliner to get that, then so be it.

When morning came, Phainon went to clock in to HQ, volunteering his day off to train new cadets. This was a nice plan. Those young kids care more about the Okhema Gladiators game than they do about celebrity gossip. The simulators were time-consuming enough to distract him from the hollow in his chest, and the nap pod near the training room was a perfect place to sleep at night.

This was a safe place to be off-grid.

Some Ground Crew Members who knew him eyed him with questions, while others directly wondered why he was there. Phainon only smiled. He lied through his teeth.

He was surprised by how easy lying had become.

And so, as Monday came, he jumped back into the hamster wheel that was his job.

While multiple short legs felt like a marathon, ultra-long-haul flights offered a different kind of torture—a sixteen-hour game between keeping his eyes on the throttle, lulled by the stagnant, hypnotizing hum of the machine during his rotation, or half-sleeping in a coffin-sized crew bunk during his off time.

Between the hassle of takeoff and landing, there was so little to do, and so much time to think about the impending doom of his relationship.

His life felt too much like cruising on autopilot, now. There are so many people on board, and yet he felt so alone. Phainon had stopped replying to his friends’ messages asking about his well-being, beyond an “I’m fine, how are you?” He used what little remained of his energy to respond to Mydei’s message, who was still telling him about his days, sending him selfies, and sharing everything he had done to fill the gap during his absence.

Which, honestly, felt more obligatory now.

He returned with the same dry enthusiasm. Maintaining his jokes, teases, flirtations, all the sweet things that felt like a love letter from Icarus to the sun. It was nice while it lasted, but soon enough, as Icarus flew any closer, he would burn.

Because he never meant to be in the sky.

It was stupid enough for Icarus to think he ever belonged in the sky.

He still loved Mydei, sure. But Phainon knew his place. He knew that he wasn’t enough for Mydei. He never would be enough, compared to Robin or Misia or whoever celebrity out there. Mydei would be better off with them. He didn’t know it yet now, but soon as Phainon was out of his sight, he would see it.

But he couldn’t give that thought, away now. Because then Mydei would be stupid about it. He’d threaten to stop everything, and the collapse of the whole campaign, the PR disaster that would follow, the fall of Chrysos Records and Sons of Gorgo and everything, would be all Phainon’s fault.

Phainon couldn’t allow that to happen.

He couldn’t drag Mydei down.

It would hurt both of them, but Mydei would move on.

He would be alright.

Over the past few days, Mydei has asked multiple times whether Phainon is ready to talk about it. Phainon only said, “later. We could talk about it when we meet. It’ll be alright.”

A lie he repeated so often, he started to believe it.

Because soon enough, the bombardment of the PR stunt did not even faze him anymore.

The mention of Robin as Queen Gorgo’s future daughter-in-law, as the universe will. He was alright with it.

The image of Mydei and Robin on the billboard. The tabloid cover of them together, the Blow Me Away music video that was played everywhere, showing Mydei and Robin holding each other, gazing at each other’s eyes, with Robin as a goddess and Mydei in his Greek Regalia that was once inhabited in his fantasy…

It was alright.

He didn’t feel anything anymore.

He walked past everything like an average person watching another celebrity on the screen.

Because that was what they were—he was an average person, and Mydei a celebrity.

Mydei’s choker was still there, latched to his neck despite the fashion he wore. But it meant nothing for Phainon now. His story was overwritten, and with how much it was shoved to him, how much he lied about it, Mydei

would soon believe it too. He would soon fully integrate into that world on the other side of Phainon’s metaphorical glass walls.

And the Mydei he knew, the Mydei he betrayed with his lies, was reduced to a couple of pixelated words on his phone screen, occasional blurred selfies, and choppy calls tainted with exhaustions and unspoken accusations.

The line grew quieter and quieter between them, but Phainon had made peace with it, too.

He had mentally prepared for that possibility so that he wouldn’t be completely pathetic when it happened. He would hold his head high, smile through it, and perhaps, if Mydei allowed him, give him the last hug, before they forever part ways, and Phainon would be a nameless face among many —a ghost in Mydei’s private history.

It was hurt, at first. He cried whenever he thought about it. But Phainon ran over that scenario in his mind over and over again, until it no longer stirred his heart.

On the second day of his rest in the layover hotel in Sigonia, Phainon got a call from Cartonus, who said that his commissioned rings, the ones he had matched with Mydei, were ready. He just had to come to the shop for the final fitting on his own ring.

Phainon was so caught up with all the fake-relationship stunts that he completely forgot about the commission. Forgot about his intention to actually propose to Mydei.

He stared at the photo Cartonus had sent: a set of rings he had commissioned for Mydei featured a blue gemstone, the color of Phainon’s eyes, a metaphor for the world, because Phainon would carry it for Mydei. Give him the world, as he promised.

And his own ring had a golden gemstone in the exact shade of Mydei’s eyes —a metaphor for the sun. A reminder of the name Mydei gave him, the name whispered to him in the most intimate moment. Fos mou—my light.

Why did he even call Phainon my light? Why did Phainon never ask?

He pondered that question once, but decided that it was far too late to even think about it. He continued to admire the rings. They were beautiful. It was Cartonus, after all. His craft was always great. But even then, it felt like a mockery to Phainon’s pain.

He mourned and was grateful in equal measure for the missed chance to propose to Mydei.

What would Mydei be, if he stuck forever with someone like Phainon?

Phainon paid Cartonus the remaining bill, asking him to keep the rings for him in the meantime. He didn’t know how long the meantime would be. He didn’t know if he’d ever picked them up. He wouldn’t know what to do with them if he did.

He put his phone down, asking Velite, his fellow pilot, the cost of a 1 LDK apartment rent near the Okhema Airport while Mydei and Robin’s music video played on the pub’s TV screen.

Phainon didn’t even turn his head. He was too busy thinking about the probability of moving.

The world spun around him so fast, and suddenly, he was dragging his suitcase across Okhema Airport.

Strangely enough, despite the numbness that had clouded his mind for the past ten days, he still dreaded coming back to that apartment. He didn’t know what he feared more: seeing Mydei… or the suffocating emptiness of home. The skeletons of the trust they once had, or the ghost of what once lived there.

But he braved himself. It’s where most of his stuff was, after all.

As he opened the door, he walked into Mydei sitting on the couch of their living room, with a half-empty bottle of Ambrosia in front of him. He bowed his head so deeply that his wild blond mane covered his face. Most

of his clothes were scattered on the floor around him, leaving him only in his black silk pants.

He looked vulnerable. Like an angel with broken wings.

Mydei shot his head up when he heard the door open, his flushed face lit up as their eyes met.

“HKS, is that really you?” his voice was deep, hoarse, slurred. Relief washed over him when he blinked and saw Phainon like he saw the sun. “Oh, thank fuck it’s you.”

Before Phainon could say anything, before he could even say hello, Mydei pulled him into a hug, chuckling as he scattered butterfly kisses across his face.

“I miss you, I miss you, I miss you, fos mou,” he whispered. His voice was shaky, like he was crying.

Phainon chuckled. “You always call me that,” he said. “But I thought I never ask what it means.”

“Because sun,” Mydei coughed, the tips of his fingers brushing on Phainon’s tattoo. “Eyes. Soul. Heart like the sun. My sun."

Phainon’s smile faltered while Mydei whispered more words in Kremnoans, the ones Phainon didn’t know. He pressed his lips on Phainon’s sun tattoo, then he stopped.

“Oh,” he sighed. “I forgot. Here. Look at me.”

He pulled something from his pants pocket. A black tiny tube that turned out to be a bright red lipstick, once he pulled the cap. Mydei let out a cheeky sneer as he put it on him.

He looked so carefree, so tipsy, that Phainon almost felt like this was one of his better dreams, if it weren’t for the sharp musk of Mydei’s perfume mixed with his sweat.

“Remember that photo of Samoyed with red lipstick all over his fur?” he chuckled. He looked a little like Queen Gorgo now. Blonde hair, confident sneer, wild eyes, red lips. He looked too much like a celebrity. “Watch me remake that now.”

He pressed his lips all across Phainon’s face, on his hair, on the corner of his eyes, leaving a sticky, oily feeling on Phainon’s skin like airport stamps. And it would have been cute, it would have been sexy if it weren’t for the fact that Mydei’s face was red.

And not in a way that he’s flushed by alcohol.

Mydei, like most Kremnoans that Phainon knew, had a high tolerance of substances. Half a bottle of Ambrosia wouldn’t get him this bad.

His cheeks and eyes were red, as if he had been crying.

“‘Dei…”

“Ssh,” Mydei chuckled. “You’re so pretty, fos mou.”

My light. And Phainon should answer it with Yours, Kotik.

Could he? Did he still have the right to say so?

“I missed you so much. ‘t feels like you’re there in the sky and I can’t fucking reach you. Why are you always so far away on the other side of the world?”

The accusation and the nickname somehow pulled out the dread from Phainon’s stomach. He tried to pull away, but Mydei caged him on the spot, burying his face on Phainon’s nape.

“By Strife, your smell,” he whispered. “It’s been so so long. Do you want to feel good? Let me make you feel good, ‘kay? Let me take care of’ya.”

Mydei dropped to his knees before Phainon could stop him, struggling to loosen Phainon’s belt with his head half clouded. He gave up halfway and just mouthed on Phainon’s pants. He chuckled when Phainon shivered.

“I can make ‘im red too now,” he cupped Phainon’s bulge. Mydei looked so childish, so innocent, so wrong. He pressed his nose to Phainon’s pants’ zipper. Oh, no. He’s not…

“‘Dei! No,” Phainon hissed, trying to haul him back up. “Don’t do that. You’ve got a tour coming on. You’ll hate it when you’re sober and your throat is busted.”

“Fuck the show,” Mydei growled, eyes flashing as he clung harder. “Please, for once, let me have this, please, please, fos mou.”

The plea in his voice, the desperation in Mydei’s eyes as he tried to mouth Phainon’s bulge, it broke Phainon’s heart. But he couldn’t do that. Mydei’s throat could go sore. He had a tour coming up. He couldn’t let ruin Mydei’s career because of his drunken antics.

“Yes, Kotik, sure. But not tonight—”

“Is it b’cause the lipstick? You hate it? We’ll ditch it,” he wiped his lips with his hand roughly, smearing it further across his cheek. He started to look wilder now.

“No, it’s not that. You’ve got a show tomorrow, right? We could just—”

Mydei’s eyes flickered with something raw: like a mix of hurt, shame, and betrayal.

As if he couldn’t believe that Phainon had rejected him.

Phainon’s breath hitched. But he did not even have time to speak as Mydei pushed to his feet.

“Fine, get the fuck off me,” he growled, the red color of shame smeared over his cheeks as he grabbed the Ambrosia’s bottle back. “If my career is more important to you than me, then fine, I’ll get the fuck out.”

“‘Dei, c’mon, I’m just taking care of you.”

“Yeah, cause that’s all you do, isn’t it? Taking care of me. You’ve used that reason to lie to my face. Why not deny me with such heroic reason, too, right?” he chuckled bitterly. “All for Mydeimos Gorgo’s sake. For his career. Cause he’s nothing without all of that crap.”

Phainon clenched his jaws. “You’re rambling now, ‘Dei,” he said. “Please, we’re both exhausted. Please don’t do this.”

“Then when are we gonna do this?” Mydei barked back, mocking Phainon in his own words. “You think I’m gonna let you run away from me another week? Another month? Another year? Are you gonna keep lying to me? Punishing me for my slip-up, even though I fucking hold the end of my deal?”

Phainon’s brain scrambled. What the fuck did he mean by slip up? He didn’t make any sense. Was he more drunk than Phainon thought?

“You’re drunk, ‘Dei,” Phainon said, in the absence of a better thing to say.

“And you’re a coward, Khaslana!” Mydei shouted. “You lied, and you ran away instead of facing me. You think I didn’t know you swapped your schedule for a sixty-two-hour round-trip flight? You signed in to your email on my phone! I see every request you send to the scheduler!”

Phainon gaped. Mydei still glared at him with the fierceness of a lion. But there was a hurt, kicked little kitten in the fire of his golden eyes, the pain that Phainon could feel in the marrow of his bones.

“‘Dei…”

“Did you think you’d got me fooled, huh?” he scoffed. “What’s in it to you anyway, Phainon? Why is it so important for you that I keep this collab? What is it with that obsession to ‘live my mother’s legacy’? Am I not worthy to even look at without her shadows over me?”

Phainon’s eyes widened, and his mind flashed back to the taxi driver’s mention. To Mydei’s self-deprecating words in the studio when they talk about the music video.

My entire career is built on a woman’s legacy. People already call me Mama’s boy, anyway.

He’s nothing like Queen Gorgo. He’s not as talented. Too bad she’s knocked up so early…

“No, ‘Dei,” Phainon croaked. His throat tightened. “I’ve seen you in the studio. You were beaming. Happy. Alive. That’s all I ever want for you. To be happy.”

“Right, and it gets you a free pass to decide what happiness is for me?” Mydei shouted. “Because only you get to decide what I should get for happiness, O Holy Deliverer?”

His condescending voice tasted so bitter in his throat that it hurt him so bad that Phainon clenched his jaws. “No, shut up, you fuckin’ brute. You dragged me to Mnestia Tower, not giving me any damn clue what you’d asked. I wasn’t prepared! You dove headfirst into this idea of collaboration, knowing that I would not have the heart to reject you in front of those people. You only wanted me there to nod along!” he gritted his teeth. “You’ve done it anyway with or without my permission!”

“Fuck you. I was hoping that the idea of me being in a relationship with someone would make you stop me,” he said. “But no, of course not. You didn’t even flinch at that idea!”

“And I’ve suffered for it!” Phainon shouted. “I’ve gotten what I deserve with every pain I see you walking around with a goddamn pop star, if that’s what you want.”

“You didn’t have to!” Mydei retorted. “We could have put a stop to it. And then you act as if nothing happened and instead decide to lie to my face. Because my dead mother’s legacy is far more important to you than our relationship.”

"Stop saying like you know shit about me, Mydeimos! Stop saying shit about me not loving you because you know damn well that’s not true,” Phainon shouted now. He could feel tears streaming down his cheek. “I’m

sorry if I make mistakes. I’m sorry I can’t love you right. I’m sorry, I don’t fucking know how to love a Concorde. I’m sorry I keep you on the ground instead of flying you high like you meant to be, cause I suck. Cause I come from the other side of the wall and can never understand you!”

His words hitched by the fresh wave of tears. Phainon did not know how to say it in the non-aviation analogy. He’s tired, confused, and his heart is breaking into a million pieces he couldn’t begin to comprehend.

“You’re rambling, Khaslana.”

“And you’re better off with someone else!”

Phainon’s words echo in the room, and Mydei flinched. His eyes widened. His clenched jaws, his balled fists, everything was let loose in the face of Phainon’s words.

No.

“Mydei—”

“Tell me you don’t mean it,” Mydei said. “Look at me and tell me, Phainon."

He wanted to take that back. He wanted to apologize, kneel, and do anything to take that back. But Phainon froze where he stood, his words hanging in the air.

And Mydei took his silence as an answer.

“So that’s it?” Mydei asked. His voice was weaker, a sign of surrender. “So that’s how it’s gonna be? You’re just gonna give up?”

Phainon knew he had to say something. He had to fight for his relationship. But he had rehearsed this in his mind, and in all of his scenarios, he gave him up.

Because he never thought that Mydei would ever want him to stay.

He never thought that Mydei was insecure about his mother. He never thought that behind Mydei’s cool rockstar bravado, he hid that kind of feeling.

All he thought was that he didn’t deserve to be with someone like Mydei.

And maybe it was the truth, like the fact that Phainon didn’t know Mydei all that well was also the truth.

“Whatever happened with you being willing to make it work?” Mydei scoffed. “Coward.”

Mydei turned around, and Phainon knew he had to stop him. He had to speak now, or he’d forever lose him. Mydeimos Gorgo. The love of his life. The owner of the ring that Phainon had commissioned, Cartonus, the man for whom he would do anything in this world, was walking out without looking back.

“‘Dei…”

His voice was too weak.

“Mydei, wait—”

But he was a bit too late. Mydei slammed the door behind him, leaving Phainon alone, among the ruins of what once was their sanctuary.

Chapter End Notes

The better part is coming I promise!

Thank you for reading!

chapters.title: Chapter 6: Mirror
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Phainon dealt with Post-breakup hollowness and found his answer in an unexpected way.

Chapter Notes

Hi! Apologies for the long, long chapter! I did promise that this will be the last, but then it got so long that I have to split it in two chapters so it's not too exhausting to read. Also, as always, a big thank you for my girl Norii for going through through this journey :D I owe you a wholleee lot for this! >.<

I hope you enjoy it!!

Phainon froze where Mydei left him, gaze fixated on the polished wood of their door as the heavy silence stretched, tearing his heart in pieces.

He should chase Mydei, pull him back, apologize—they could fix this, because they’re stronger than any PR stunt, and Phainon promised to be the best boyfriend who ever existed.

And yet he didn’t move.

Seconds stretched, pulling Mydei further away from him. Phainon knew that it would be too late to run to get Mydei now, but he could still call him, beg him to stay, text him a string of apologies, send out voice notes, anything, anything to tell Mydei that he wanted to fix this. He wanted them to stay together.

Still, he didn’t move.

Phainon wasn’t sure if he still had the right to do it.

Because he was the one who pushed Mydei into the fake relationship, despite Mydei repeatedly offering to end it, he insisted on enduring it, even though he was troubled. He was the one who lied, despite Mydei begging him to be honest. He was the one who denied him, despite Mydei’s desperation.

The image of Mydei’s drunken smile automatically replayed by his mind in slow motion, how his expression turned into shock, into a shame that flushed his skin as he realized that Phainon rejected him, the anger that bubbled under his skin, and exploded in Phainon’s face…

You’re a coward, Khaslana. He was. He knew he was.

You don’t even care. Wrong. He cared too much; he would give Mydei everything.

Am I not worthy to even look at without her shadows? Phainon never even liked Queen Gorgo’s music. He didn’t know who she was before he came to Okhema.

Get the fuck off me. Was that your wish, too? Because Phainon would do it. He would disappear if that were what Mydei wanted.

No, he was gone. They were done.

It was all over.

The realization punched air out of him. Phainon’s vision began to blur as his mind replayed that word over and over.

Mydei wouldn’t come back.

It crushed him, as if the world had collapsed onto his chest; how alone he was, how suffocating this room that was supposed to be his home. How foreign was this place where he once slept next to his favorite warmth and ate homemade food made by caring hands.

The caring hands were far out of his reach now.

Phainon had thought about this a million times over for the past week. He knew it would happen. It was just too obvious. Mydei was a star—born for the world to admire him. And Phainon was just… well, Phainon. A country boy from Aedes Elysiae who once dared to challenge him and somehow stayed.

It never mattered how much he tried to be worthy of Mydei, because they were not the same; they would never stand as equals.

And yet, why did it hurt so much?

Was it because his incompetence felt so public? Like, instead of a private confirmation of his inadequacy to be with Mydei, the whole world told him that there will always be someone who is better than him. The entire world reminded him how small and unimportant he was. No matter what he did, he would never be like Robin.

Were their endless words on social media hurt his ego so bad that it hurt so much?

Why did it bother him? They were not wrong.

Did it even matter? His ego? Their opinions? What did it matter now that Mydei’s gone?

He’s gone.

And he’s not going away in a quiet aloofness that Phainon always imagined Mydei would be. He walked away, betrayed. Denied. His accusatory words bounced inside Phainon’s empty head, the image of his angry face plastered on the back of his eyelids, burned there like a brand.

You hurt him.

He wouldn’t hurt for long. Mydei would be okay. The whole world loved him.

Still, you hurt him.

Mydei was drunk. He was probably just pent-up, exhausted, and emotional.

You said you’d be the best boyfriend ever.

Phainon could be wrong. He could overestimate himself. He tended to do that. He was once convinced that he could fly a Concorde, only to have his dream crushed because he had to pack so many hours before he could even dream of taking the exam, and by the time Phainon could do it, Concorde was officially grounded forever.

What does it matter now, anyway? Mydei’s gone. His promise meant nothing.

Nothing mattered anymore.

He’s gone. He’s gone.

Phainon walked to the couch where Mydei sat earlier, curling himself into a fetal position as he pressed his face to the soft fabric, engulfing himself in the remains of Mydei’s presence. He could feel it gradually dampened by his tears. By the time he realized he was crying, his tears dropped uncontrollably, and Phainon screamed into the cushion, sobbing as he poured the pent-up emotions he had bottled up since Kephale knew when.

But even his voice was swallowed by the silence, reminding him how alone he was now.

How lonely he felt.

Phainon cried until the pain somehow numbed, reduced into a pulsing pain in his chest, a stinging pain in his eyes, and the paralysis that he couldn’t quite understand. He couldn’t remember when he stopped crying, or how time seemed to move in a strange velocity, because when he blinked and saw his surroundings, sunlight had filled the room with its bright light.

And everything stayed the same: the stillness, the emptiness, the pain that echoed in the silence.

Mydei had truly gone.

Phainon flipped so he lay on his back now, staring at the crystal chandeliers hanging on the high ceiling. The golden, branch-like frame resembled a tree limb, cascading into a dramatic array of clear crystal droplets that reflected sunlight from the window and mimicked the look of morning dew or icicles. The warm lighting looked pale compared to the sun, yet it cast a soft glow reminiscent of the first dawn of spring.

It was a chandelier that Mydei bought in Aidonia; its delivery fee nearly matched the price. Phainon had made a fuss, jokingly scolding him for not buying one from YAYKEA like a normal person.

“This reminds me of your Mom’s backyard tree in Aedes Elysiae,” Mydei said with a straight face. He stared at the lamp with his arms crossed in front of his chest, a slight tug of a smile on his lips. “I thought your Mom and Dad would appreciate it if they came over. It’ll help make them feel like this is their home, too, don’t you think?”

Whatever joke that Phainon meant to retort him, whatever word he thought, died on his tongue that day. He stared at Mydei, who looked so soft, at peace, gazing at the small piece of Aedes Elysiae in their apartment as if he were reminiscing about home.

Phainon was totally flabbergasted, totally moved by the view in front of him, and the question popped into his mind before he could even stop it.

Marry me, Mydeimos.

Because he thought it might mean that Mydei wanted permanence, that Mydei wished to build a family. Phainon was so in awe, so invested in that idea that he commissioned the rings from Cartonus. He spent the entire three days of his Mandatory Rest Day looking up the right reference for the rings.

But now that he thought about it again, maybe he was wrong. Maybe Mydei didn’t mean it that way at all. Maybe he was just so mesmerized by Aedes Elysiae's nature and wanted a little piece of it at home. Maybe Mydei was just trying to be nice to Phainon’s parents.

Ah, well, it didn’t matter now.

Mydei had gone.

Phainon stared and stared and stared and stared, his mind wandering everywhere. He wondered if they would still be fine if Phainon had said no to Mydei’s demand to be in a fake relationship, back in the Mnestia Tower. If they still had their sanctuary, safe and sound, without the unnecessary noises that push them away from each other.

But then again, he would never have seen Mydei’s face lit up, childlike and alive. He wouldn’t have a chance to hear Mydei talk about music so enthusiastically, and Mydei wouldn’t have any chance to see his mother’s legacy come to life. The great, talented Mydeimos Gorgo would be forever locked to the ground. The Concorde that was destined to reach greatness would never soar to the sky …

But they’ll still be together.

No, Phainon could never dare to do that to Mydei, even if Mydei thought that it was what he wanted.

Mydeimos Gorgo was destined to be so much more than just some nobody’s boyfriend.

“I’ll give you the world,” Phainon’s croaked voice whispered to the still air that swallowed his words into silence. “Even if I have to burn myself trying.”

Phainon let out a weak, defeated smile. It’s no use thinking about what could have been.

A new dawn had come.

All he could do now was just face the consequences of his choice and move on with his life.

Phainon got up from where he lay, not sure what to do. Now that the sun of a new day illuminated the room, he felt even more like a stranger in this

house. Everything he thought of doing felt intrusive; he didn’t feel like he could eat Mydei’s pre-made food in the fridge, or use his kitchen to make breakfast. It felt even more wrong to think of brushing his teeth or taking a shower in the master bedroom.

It felt like he was overstaying his welcome, cause this wasn’t his home anymore.

So Phainon got up, picking up Mydei’s clothes on the floor, every piece was a Dollywood glam that Mydei had stripped himself of—a mask he bared before he faced Phainon. He then picked up the shattered Ambrosia bottle, piece by piece, not caring that some of the sharp edges scraped his skin a little.

Mydei hated Ambrosia.

He hated the effect on his body, since he always treated it like a sacred temple. They only keep alcohol in the house to welcome guests. Why did he drink it now? What happened before he came home? Why did Mydei come home drunk and all over him like he was desperate?

Phainon’s eyes locked onto the small black tube with a bright red tip smudging the floor. He picked up the lipstick, wiping off the half-crushed bullet, and noticed only a silver engraving on the base: a star and the letter R in a fancy font.

Robin.

Phainon remembered this lipstick, now. It was a special collaboration item. Phainon had seen the advertising for the lipstick so many times in the airport’s makeup stores.

Why did Mydei want to mark Phainon in Robin’s color? Did the ruse finally get to him? And he realized when he came home that he wished Robin instead of him, so he wanted to paint Phainon in her color. Was it Mydei’s final attempt to make Phainon worthy in his world?

What happened?

Phainon sighed, placing the lipstick on the island between the kitchen and the living room.

As much as he wanted answers, it’s no use to cling to those questions now. It was all over.

He moved around the house, getting hangers from the guest bedroom to place Mydei’s Dollywood clothes: the red satin tuxedo jacket, white silk shirts, white cravats. Phainon would put it in the laundry, but he wasn’t sure how to handle it. Mydei’s costumes usually had a particular way to clean.

Another proof that Phainon couldn’t ever understand Mydei’s world.

Phainon left to take a shower in the guest’s shower room, and when he finally saw his reflection in the mirror, Phainon nearly burst back into tears.

He looked like a complete mess. His eyes were red and puffy, and there were still red stains in the shape of Mydei’s lips all across his skin; smeared and faded in a few spots, but the mark was so visible that it shattered the pieces he tried to put together.

The image of Mydei’s hurt and betrayal played in his mind again, but this time, Phainon allowed his heart to just break. He allowed himself to accept that he would live with that guilt for the rest of his life; he had denied Mydeimos Gorgo, the man with whom his heart ached.

He deserved it.

Phainon ran the shower and let the cold water wash off the last remnants of Mydei on his body. He cried as the red on his skin wiped clean, and when he stepped out of the shower, he had no more tears to shed; the pain had all washed off the drain.

It felt so utterly, completely hollow, like he was nothing but an empty shell.

But maybe it gave him room for a new beginning.

To move forward, start by leaving this place.

Phainon used the spare clothes from his work suitcase for the day and packed the rest. He glanced at the door to their shared room, wondering if he should go there to pick up another set of clean uniforms and some of his important documents; his flight certificates, some clean pairs of underwear and boxers, perhaps his shaving kit…

No.

He couldn’t enter that room.

He had just lost Mydei. He couldn’t lose the memory of his sanctuary, too.

Not now, at least.

Maybe much later, he could ask their cleaner to help collect Phainon’s personal belongings. Maybe much later, he could ask Mydei to let him drop by to pick them up. Maybe much, much later, if enough time passed, they could become friends. Maybe Mydei would let him hang around the house again, even if only for a few hours.

The thought made Phainon scoff.

He was certain that he couldn’t just be friends with Mydei. Their world was too different, and he loved that man too much. He couldn’t even imagine seeing Mydei with someone else, even if he knew that it was inevitable.

Phainon zipped his suitcase and walked to the door. He looked back at the house for the last time: the modern living room with a contemporary lamp casting a warm glow. The kitchen with a complete set of utensils and spices, the wall-sized glass window that views the city, the dark wooden door to their room… a place he shared with the love of his life.

For the last time, Phainon smiled at the room, a quiet salute for everything they once shared.

Then, he walked out the door, feeling his heart shatter as the soft click was heard behind him.

Goodbye, sanctuary.

Phainon had no other place to go in Okhema that did not include Mydei in any way. Not his friends, not Aglaea’s. So he decided to clock in to work, volunteering himself to help mentor young cadets in the simulation training.

He distracted himself from the gaping wound in his heart by standing at the edge of the simulator bay, watching as two cadets fumbled through pre-flight checklists on the overhead panel. Their voices echoed with too much energy for this hour.

“Checklist complete!” one young cadet said, a bit too proudly.

Phainon leaned in from behind the seat and pointed at the center console. “Uh-huh…” he said. “And what about the APU bleed?”

The cadet whipped his head so quickly and crushed quietly. Haikas.

Phainon short-circuited as his half-sutured heart was ripped off again.

“Hey, no cursing in my sim bay, young man,” he scolded, before his brain could register it.

The young man looked at him, startled. “Sir, you… know Kremnoan?”

Yeah, from being called that affectionately for four years. But Phainon only shrugged.

“I’ve flown to Castrum Kremnos several times, kid. Of course, I know a curse word or two,” he said jokingly, ignoring the metaphorical bleeding in his chest. “Now repeat from the beginning. Don’t forget the APU Bleed lest we’ll get a bad review from the hot cabin, okay?”

The young cadet shouted a loud ‘Yes, Sir!’, and Phainon’s day continued. Come nighttime, he slept at the nap bay again, and the next day, he volunteered to sim program again, much to the young cadets’ excitement. He was grateful for their enthusiasm. It could somehow help manage the persistent dull ache in his chest that refused to go away.

On his last Mandatory Rest Day, though, Eleanor, the HR manager, came to the nap bay herself to hand Phainon the permission to mentor the simulator bay, but not without a gentle reminder that his ground work will be accumulated to his work hours this month, and gave him a very friendly reminder to use his rest days by resting appropriately.

Phainon only nodded, but his mind said otherwise.

He didn’t need rest. He needed a distraction.

Eleanor looked like she knew she was being ignored, because she crossed her arms, ready to lecture Phainon about how important rest was for the sake of a safe flight. But Phainon excused himself before she could say anything. He had been flying for so many hours. He knew when he was rested enough to fly another short leg rotation without collapsing.

Besides, Eleanor shouldn’t be that offended.

She was not the only person Phainon chose to ignore.

He ignored voicemails from Caelus and Dan Heng, who told him they should really hang out (Caelus) and that they were super worried about him (Dan Heng). He ignored Stelle’s texts, which ranged from questions and demands to threats to pick up her calls. He ignored even Anaxa’s invitation to dinner together with Hyacine and Castorice the next time he was in town. All with many variations of the simple sentence:

Sorry, can’t. It’s a crazy time at work. Next time, yeah?

He couldn’t do that to Cyrene, though, so every time she asked for a call, Phainon would call her, as briefly as he could. He tried to keep the conversation about work and home, but of course, Cyrene was sharper than

that. She kept asking about Mydei, and Phainon answered as best he could without giving away their breakup.

He couldn’t bring himself to mention his name.

Maybe someday, when he could meet Cyrene in person. But in the meantime, he’d pretended that nothing happened.

“Phainon, you can’t keep avoiding me like this,” Cyrene said. Of course, he would hear the words he didn’t say. Of course, she would confront him about it. “Please, let’s meet up and talk? Tomorrow is my last day in Okhema. Who knows when we could see each other again?”

“I have a rotation tomorrow, Cy,” Phainon said, staring at the dull roof of the nap bay. “I’m sorry. I’ll come home the next time, okay?”

There was a silence on the other side of the line, the kind that Cyrene usually liked to hold to make Phainon feel like he had to fill it with additional reasons. But Phainon was ragged by suppressed sorrow and exhaustion. He‘d let the silent stretch as long as she wants.

“Phainon,” Cyrene finally submitted. “Don’t be like that.”

“Don’t be like what?”

“You’ve been avoiding everyone. Caelus. Cas. Hyacinthia, and Stelle, and Mydei…”

Phainon could feel his heart leap. He could feel it skip a beat, hearing Mydei’s name being mentioned. But he held it in. “What, you’ve been talking about me?” he chuckled, but no humor was heard from his exhausted voice.

“Phai, we don’t live in a cave. We know what’s happening out there with Mydei and Robin,” Cyrene insisted. “The news is everywhere, and suddenly you’re too busy to meet anyone or even to call anyone. So I gotta call Mydei and…”

Cyrene sighed, as if weighing her next words.

Phainon raised his brows. “... And?”

The line went silent. Phainon had to look at his phone screen to see whether Cyrene had hung up or if the line was cut.

“Cy? Did he tell you?”

There was a sigh, a sign of surrender and frustration. “Snowy, you’re my little brother,” she said. “Why are you doing this to me? Don’t you even want to talk about it to your big sis?”

Oh, Kephale, no, he did not need this.

Phainon could feel a lump in his throat. No, he didn’t want to talk about it, cause then it would feel too real, and Phainon wasn’t ready for that. Not now. Not today.

Maybe not ever. But Cyrene wouldn’t let his silence linger that long.

So he would hold what he could right now.

“I uh…” Phainon let out a long, shaky sigh, swallowing the sob. “I’ll tell you later, yeah? I can’t do it now. I have an early flight tomorrow.”

“Snowy, please,” she said quietly. “I’m worried about you so so much.”

“What did he tell you?” he asked, half-hoping that Cyrene wouldn’t tell, half-hoping that she would. Phainon didn’t know what he wanted anymore.

“It doesn’t matter. You’re my little brother, I want to hear it from you,” Cyrene said firmly. “Come on. Talk to me.”

Phainon bit his lips, pressing his eyelids shut to keep the tears inside. He really couldn’t do this. He couldn’t talk to Cyrene because if he started now, he would cry his heart out. He couldn’t do that when he had work so early the next day.

“Sorry, Cy. I’m too exhausted to talk right now,” he said. “I’m sorry, I’ll tell you when I’m ready, yeah? I just… can’t be distracted right now. Work’s

really crazy.”

Another pause from Cyrene’s end, before she finally sighed. “Alright, fine,” she said. “But please promise me to talk to someone, okay? If you can’t talk to me, talk to Cae. Or Mom. Please call Mom. Don’t be stubborn and handle everything on your own. Sometimes a hero needs another hero, too, remember?”

Phainon couldn’t help but let out a little chuckle, and a drop of tears along with it. He wiped his cheek, smiling bitterly at himself as he heard the catchphrase their Mom constantly repeated to them when they were young, when Phainon still loved to play pretend.

It’s too late now.

He had already destroyed his relationship and himself along with it.

Only time could heal him.

“Okay, Cy, I promise,” Phainon said weakly. He didn’t mean it, but no point in making Cyrene even more worried.

“Alright,” she said. “Come home soon, City boy.”

Phainon hummed a goodbye, and then, he closed his eyes, trying to sleep off the guilt and broken heart. He thought he had gotten used to it. But each time he was alone, he could feel the cut, fresh as the night Mydei left him.

But a new dawn always comes, and he walked back into the hamster wheel that was his work again: flying regional leg, sleeping all day on standby days and layovers, another regional leg, volunteering for the sim programs or log-keeping on his Rest Days, on and on again. He kept his day moving as busy as possible, while the world spun around him, sending him a few passing news of the Royalty Tour. With every dawn, every conversation he overheard from total strangers, Mydei felt a distance further away from Phainon, going up and away to the unreachable heights.

By the time their first concert of the tour started, Mydei had skyrocketed to the sky beyond what Phainon could reach.

It stung, still. But this time, Phainon no longer had time to stop and cry.

He always had the next flight to catch. Next simulator to supervise.

In the third week since he broke up with Mydei, he was assigned an ultra-long-haul flight to Sigonia, which he gladly accepted. Phainon loved flying to Sigonia. They always have the opposite season with Okhema, and honestly, with the humid summer almost peaking in Amphoreus, the cold winter wind was a welcome change.

Since Phainon was assigned to the second shift, he practically had nothing to do until the later part of the flight. He flew more miles than he could think, and somehow, that night with Mydei still felt like yesterday. The dull ache in his chest still pulsed as if it had a life of its own, yet the distance made it feel like his happier moments with Mydei were nothing more than a vivid dream.

“Captain Khaslana, you’re up,” Velite nudged him out of his daydream. “ATC just relayed light turbulence ahead. Weather’s shifting, too.”

As passengers began to deboard, Nymphas stepped into the cockpit, offering him a polite smile as she asked if a little girl and her fathers from First Class could come to the cockpit and take a picture.

The door opened, and the girl bounded inside with an innocent enthusiasm. Blond hair in soft waves, violet eyes wide with awe.

She reminded Phainon of someone else he had met, that somehow made his heart feel strange.

Dr. Ratio and Aventurine.

Aventurine.

Of all people.

The man who reduced Mydei into moodboards and narratives…

The man whose ideas made Mydei bowed in their living room, drunk and crying.

If it weren’t because of you… If it weren’t because of your stupid idea…

Accidental kiss.

And while Phainon allowed himself to drown in his own insecurities, while he was swept away by a stream of words and pseudo-psychological analysis in his own head, Mydei had tried to keep his promise even harder than Phainon could imagine.

Oh, Kephale.

Aventurine smirked, looking half-amused, half-baffled. “Holy shit, you’re the one breaking up with him,” he said. “My dear Captain, you’re so oblivious, aren’t you?”

Phainon scoffed. “It doesn’t matter now.”

Even in his own ears, he sounded so broken, so hurt that it silenced Aventurine. It’s strange to see this taunting master at a loss for words.

“Oh, I’m sure it matters a lot for Mydei,” Aventurine said. “Is the kiss really making you uncomfortable, Phainon? Did you really go and date a celebrity without even a single thought that he’d kiss someone else for the art? Are you really so naive?”

Phainon’s heart almost imploded in his chest. It’s not even about the kiss, he wanted to scream. He had only known about it just now. He didn’t know to make a fuss about it because…

… by the time of that gala, he had already turned away from Mydei-related news.

He had completely turned away from Mydei.

And not because he wanted to go off-grid, as Dan Heng suggested. But because deep down, he had already been so convinced that they were over. He had already distanced himself from Mydei while he was still fighting tooth and nail for it. Mydei was still throwing a fit about the accidental kiss, worrying about what Phainon would think, while Phainon was rehearsing his goodbye.

But was Phainon even in the wrong? He was only thinking he was doing Mydei a favor. That removing himself from the picture was what was best for Mydei’s happiness and career.

… And it gets you a free pass to decide what happiness is for me?

Mydei’s angry words bounced inside Phainon’s skull, so loud that it almost deafened him. Phainon pressed his eyes shut, pressing the bridge of his nose.

“Look, Mydei’s free now. He can be the star he’s meant to be without me dragging him down,” Phainon said, his voice brittle. “I just came here to tell you—don’t ever do that to him again. Don’t push him into something that sends him home drunk and crying. You promised you’d stop the moment Mydei got hurt.”

“Oh, Captain, but it’s not my plan that hurt him that day,” Aventurine said calmly. “He went completely livid because he thought he hurt you. He yelled at everyone to cut that scene, to make it disappear ASAP, but it already went viral, and he still went on a rampage, yelling about how to fix it.”

Aventurine narrowed his eyes, and the smirk faltered as he continued.

“He had been excessively annoying about the plan since Owlbert’s show. Still smart, but even I sense desperation in his actions. Like he was taking a shot in the dark about what might upset you, and cutting it out preemptively. It’s almost sad, really. Like you never told him what you were actually uncomfortable with. So he had to guess on his own.”

Bullseye.

It hit right on the spot that Phainon couldn’t even deny it. Even his dismissive scoff sounded weak.

And Aventurine seemed to know that, too.

“Wow, damn, Captain,” Aventurine laughed, but there was no humor in it, just disbelief twisted into something cruel. “I can’t believe I thought Mydei had everything. Brawn, beauty, brain, and a chill, understanding partner to boot. Boy, I hate it when I’m wrong.”

“I endured it for him,” Phainon said. “I endured everything, so I don’t hold him back.”

“And nobody said you should,” Aventurine retorted sharply. “Don’t you remember? The deal was that this would all stop the moment you’re uncomfortable with it. It had happened with the Dr. Markenz campaign. Mydei asked us to stop, so we did. I paid half of the penalty, too. You have that kind of power, Phainon. Mydei had declared it to everyone that day. Yet you chose to endure it instead. And look where that unnecessary self-sacrifice got you.”

Look where it got Mydei, was implied. But Aventurine was kind enough to hold his tongue.

Phainon gritted his teeth; his jaws hurt. But he couldn’t retort to that, because Aventurine was right about him. He was right about Mydei, too. Phainon couldn’t help but rewind what Mydei said in their car, back after the meeting in Mnestia Tower.

I want you to know what we’ve gotten into, and you have to be honest about how you feel about this entire situation. The music, the legacy, they’re not more important than you.

But Phainon just wanted to make Mydei’s life easier. Make his career smoother.

“All of that, and you still push him away,” Aventurine scoffed.

He was just trying to be kind. To be understanding.

Why was he so wrong?

“Well, I’ll leave you to mull over it, then. If you’ll excuse me, my daughter is waiting,” Aventurine said, when it was clear that Phainon was too paralyzed to continue the conversation. “Also, I don’t know you, and I don’t give a damn about your feelings or your relationship. But I respect Mydeimos, so I’ll give you a little advice in his favor. Remember, there’s a reason they’re called a star. They burn in the dark—surrounded by worse devils than me, men with lesser morals and higher ambitions. So maybe tuck that insecurity back in your ass and next time, start talking like a man who knows the odds before the dark swallowed you both.”

Phainon watched as Aventurine straightened his position to leave. But before he disappeared behind the door, Phainon stopped him.

“Wait,” Phainon called, his voice rough. Aventurine stopped, glancing over his shoulder with the faintest smirk. “If Mydei had refused that day… if I’d said no to your collaboration plan, who else were you going to approach?”

The blond chuckled, tilting his head. “Truthfully? No one. Mydei was my all-or-nothing for this plan. If he had refused for any reason, I would have thought of another way to help Robin. And even if he’d quit midway, it wouldn’t pose much of a problem for me either. I’d always find a way to keep going. I’m very good at placing my bets in the right hands.”

Aventurine let the words settle, then added, almost gently.

“I do feel bad that this campaign cost him the relationship he was hell-bent on keeping. My poor little lion. But hey, maybe we could all learn our lessons here. In love, no good intentions are ever a better bet than the truth.”

Another strike to Phainon’s ego. He dug his nails so hard into his palms that he could feel a crescent shape of pain there. But he didn’t say anything.

“Huh, ain’t that something, coming from someone like me?” Aventurine laughed again before giving Phainon a salute and a wink. “Good day, captain. May your skies always be clear.”

Phainon’s breath hitched. His stomach dropped like an aircraft in sudden turbulence. For a moment, he couldn’t move, couldn’t speak. There was a

flare in his chest that came from the remnants of his broken heart. But this time it wasn’t anger—just a hollow ache gnawing at him.

And as Aventurine’s footsteps fade, he could see the images of Mydei’s hurt face again, now mixed with fear, the emotion that Phainon had missed entirely the first time he saw it.

-

Phainon didn’t even wait until he reached his layover hotel. He sat in one of the airport seats, pulled out his phone, and typed "Mydei Robin Kiss" into TabTube.

The top result was a thumbnail close-up of Mydei’s lips brushing Robin’s. Even from the still, Phainon could see the shock in Mydei’s eyes.

It was a very fancy stage. Net Gala, considering how fancy Robin looked. Mydei was wearing the red satin tux that Phainon picked up from the floor after the fight that led to their breakup.

Their performance was excellent; they sang with such fiery intensity that it was no wonder the crowd cheered so loudly. Robin and Mydei played the part of the singers who adored each other, with Mydei occasionally leaning into Robin, and Robin brushing her hands on Mydei’s shoulders every once in a while. It was all straight out of Aventurine’s moodboard.

But then, as they ended the song and Robin greeted the Dollywood elites who attended Net Gala, one of the famous producers, whose name Phainon couldn’t remember, suddenly shouted, “Now Kiss!” to which the rest of the audience parroted in a unified chant. Robin only laughed, while Mydei was busy adjusting something in his ear while looking at someone under the stage, clearly too distracted with something. He must have an issue with his noise-reduction earplugs. The shape of Mydei’s inner ears was always too big to fit some of the plugs on the market.

Robin tried to defuse it, tried to say it was inappropriate, but the audience kept roaring, kept chanting that one word.

Kiss! Kiss! Kiss! Kiss!

“Just on the cheek, yeah?” she said, finally, leaning to Mydei. She placed one hand on his shoulder and whispered something, but Mydei tilted his head in the last moment, probably to hear Robin better.

And then, it happened.

Robin’s lips brushed against Mydei’s. It was quick, subtle, even far too quick to be called a peck. But the audience roared all the same. They shouted, laughed, whistled, and clapped their hands as if they were crowning new monarchs.

But Phainon did not have the time to feel jealous. All he could see was Mydei’s face looking beet red, biting his lower lip. When they finally broke the kiss, much to the audience’s roar, Mydei looked everywhere but the camera. He could at least maintain his smile, which could be seen as a little coy, but he knew that it didn’t reach his eyes.

And Robin… she handled it better than Mydei. She laughed shyly at the camera, but Phainon could see that with every glance at Mydei, she must be quietly worried. She kept denying another kiss until the MC for the next segment had to push Mydei to kiss Robin like he meant it, to which Mydei only shrugged.

“Robin got so many young fans, Elba, come on. Let’s not teach them excess PDA, yeah?” he said. His voice trembled, but it could easily be blamed on the effect of his post-performance.

The audience laughed, and with one last wave, Mydei and Robin exited the stage.

It had fifteen million views and thousands of comments. The netizens were cheering on them with more caps locks, more #LionDove hashtags, and as

he scrolled through, he could see the #shydei and #simpdei hashtags— painting Mydei’s suppressed anger as the shy smittenness.

But no, that couldn’t be the reason why Mydei was coming home drunk.

Phainon typed Mydei Net Gala red carpet, and clicked on the longest duration he could find.

The video was a montage of multiple angles of Mydei and Robin walking on the red carpet. From their arrival in the limo to their walk, the poses in front of a bunch of cameras, and even a few interviews with him and Robin. The double interviews talked about their album, their relationship, and their outfit inspiration, which were mainly rehearsed versions of what Phainon already knew.

But as Mydei got to his solo interview, the interviewer paused, like she didn’t know what to ask now that Robin was out of the picture.

“So Mydei, that outfit is clearly Gorgo red, yeah? Is that inspired by her, too?” she asked, finally.

Am I not worthy to look at without her shadow over me?

Mydei nodded. “Yeah, definitely. The blue flowers also represented her spirit. Aglaea added it because it aligned with the Wild Hunt theme of the year. It’s from House of Goldenweaver, as usual. Aglaea did an amazing job, didn’t she?”

The interviewer asked a few more rehearsed, typical questions, which Mydei answered with ease. A short answer that he deflected to praise other parties; Ratio, Robin, his bandmates, Aventurine, all in a professional tone. But then, in the middle of the interview, someone entered the camera's field, and the man quickly put his hands around Mydei’s shoulders.

“Look at my son looking so damn good.”

Mydei’s shocked face was only there for a second, but even then, it looked a fracture too long for his usual stoic face. He glanced at Eurypon Soos, his

father, and let out a rehearsed smile.

“Hey, old man.”

The interviewer looked thrilled, probably didn’t expect that her segment would turn into an exclusive moment with Mydeimos Gorgo and his famous, legendary producer father, Eurypon Soos, in one frame. Eurypon dominates the interview for a bit. He mostly talked about how Mydei could finally live up to his Mom’s legacy now that he collaborated with Robin, how proud he was, and so many other bullshit that Phainon chose to mute.

He didn’t like Eurypon.

Mydei had briefly mentioned his relationship with Eurypon when they first started dating. Eurypon was a shitty husband to Gorgo, and even a shittier father. When Gorgo passed away, Mydei cut off relations with his father, deciding to stay with Krateros and take his mother’s last name.

“That’s a nice move,” Phainon had said then. “Mydeimos Gorgo does sound more badass than Mydeimos Soos, anyway.”

Phainon still remembered Mydei’s laugh right after he said that. His head thrown back, his mouth open, and he looked carefree, as if for a moment, he allowed himself to free himself from the weight of his parents' name.

He skipped Eurypon’s part, unable to see how exhausted Mydei looked next to his father. As Phainon fast-forwarded the video and skimmed through the interviews, he saw that most of them asked the same things: Robin, the collaboration, the outfit he wears, and his Mother’s legacy.

But never about him. Never about the music he so fantastically made.

Am I not worthy to even look at without her shadows over me?

Phainon suddenly remembered the feeling he had back in the studio on the listening party of the EP. He felt helplessly out of place, being surrounded by big names in the industry he wasn’t a part of. He remembered feeling

small, how he was just a normal human among giants, with the only reason he was there being his connection to Mydei.

What if Mydei felt the same, too?

What if he felt alone and small in such a prestigious event, because his only reason for being there was that he was Gorgo’s son?

My entire career is built on a woman’s legacy. People already call me Mama’s boy, anyway.

Mydei had said it in a flat tone, almost as if he were used to it.

Like it was a bitter truth he was forced to swallow.

Phainon pursed his bottom lip. Then, he typed another search, Mydei’s Bonk or Debunk interview. It was a talk show hosted by a comedy duo who often roasted their guests. Cyrene and Phainon were absolutely furious when they watched it together, because the comedians were particularly rude to Mydei.

“Mydei, we got someone here that says, ‘Mydeimos will never have a career without the Gorgo’.”

Mydei only laughed. “That’s true. I don’t think people will give two shits about me if not ‘cause of my Mom’s name and my bandmates’ talent.”

“Here’s another: Mydeimos doesn’t even sound good.”

“Also true, I scream better, and Peucesta sings clean better. But Peu got a condition. He couldn’t sing on stage for two hours straight for the whole tour period, so take it or leave it, f(beep)ers.”

“A son of Eurypon Soos, yet signed with Anaxa and Chrysos Records. Even your own blood doesn’t want to do anything with you.”

“That’s very rude, you should call him Anaxagoras. That’s the name he preferred,” Mydei said, much to the hosts and the audience’s laughter. “But also, Anaxagoras was a huge fan of my mom. No one understands her

vision better than him. I only want to work with those who know her best, blood or not.”

He had always said everything flatly, even with a mix of humor, like he wasn’t bothered by it.

Every album, every interview—Queen Gorgo was there, hovering like a ghost. Mydei’s voice, his lyrics, even his rage—all of it smothered under her name. Phainon realized, with a sick twist in his gut, that if the last name was removed, Mydeimos would never have existed at all.

It was always Gorgo’s son, or Mydeimos of the Sons of Gorgo.

But never just Mydeimos.

Never the man.

And only now did Phainon realize that maybe Mydei was drowning, too— but in a different kind of noise. Not in the words of gossip or tabloids, but in the impossible weight of legacy. Maybe his mother’s name was both a crown and a chain.

And Phainon, blinded by his own fear of not understanding Mydei’s legacy, had unknowingly tightened the chain.

He remembered what he said that day, right before Mydei asked for the choker: “Do it for your mom’s legacy. It’s important for me too.”

Maybe that’s why he was crying that night. That’s why he was furious.

Not because of Robin, or because he was disappointed. He must be exhausted by the pressure, by his father, and maybe by the hurt because Phainon had vanished for a week after he made false promises. Told him they’d meet on Wednesday—then took a flight to avoid him.

What if Mydei had come home hoping for sanctuary and found it empty? Mydei always hated waking up to an empty room. He must have been feeling so lonely, even amidst the noise. Because, sure, there are so many people who love him. But not because of him.

Because of the legacy he carried.

What if he saw Phainon and hoped that he could finally be just somebody’s boyfriend?

Not his mother’s successor, not his father’s son.

Not even Mydeimos Gorgo.

But Phainon’s ‘Dei, Honeycake, Kotik.

What if that was why he clung so fiercely to intimacy? He just wanted to be held as he was.

And yet Phainon kept urging him to rest, to think about the tour, kept reminding him of the career he couldn’t screw up. Even if it came from love, even if Phainon thought he was just doing his duty as a good boyfriend, it only made Phainon one more voice pushing him back into Gorgo’s shadow.

Phainon had never asked about what the legacy meant for Mydei. He only saw Mydei carrying it and pretended to understand. He generously offered to help carry that legacy, without even asking Mydei first.

And when he realized that he didn’t know how to hold it, when he thought that someone could hold it better, he chose defeat, without fighting for Mydei first. Thinking that he was doing Mydei a favor.

How stupid could he be?

Aventurine’s words rang in Phainon’s mind again. No good intentions are ever a better bet than the truth.

Phainon could feel his heart pounding faster as he realized the weight of his rejection that night.

Stupid, stupid Phainon.

He had lost count of how many videos he watched. He even watched the oldest ones when Mydei was still a child singer. When he ran out of videos, he went to the most recent ones with Robin, wondering whether they still asked about Gorgo when Mydei wasn’t the only one in the frame.

Not to his surprise, they did.

But strangely enough, Mydei was chattier in these interviews. He often shifted the conversation about his mother to praise Robin, how similar she was to the late Queen Gorgo, how she could even hit Gorgo’s signature gritty scream, one that no one had ever managed to pull off. Every praise he said pointed at Robin as his mom’s successor. The next queen of rock.

Wait.

That was all too deliberate to be random praise.

Mydei had never been so passionate like that, or talked about his mom in that way.

Phainon repeated that part over and over, where Mydei was saying that Gorgo would have loved Robin. She would have loved to place her literal crown on her instead of on him, had she ever had the chance.

People in the comments gushed over how Mydei was so in love. But Phainon could see how… strange it was. Mydei wasn’t just praising Robin’s talent, wasn’t he? It wasn’t that he fell in love with her, per se. It was—

It was as if he was projecting his Mom’s light on her, placing her legacy on Robin…

So he shouldn’t anymore.

That was a crazy theory. All the years Phainon knew Mydei, Phainon had always known how much Mydei cherished his mother’s legacy. He built his career on it. He was very careful about her legacy. He loved Gorgo so much. There’s no way he could just place it on someone else.

And yet, it clicked so well that everything seemed clearer for Phainon.

Mydei had carried it throughout his career as a child singer. And then, as he grew up, he hung out with the guys from his Mother’s philanthropic music school—the same guys she helped raise with her scholarships. That’s why they called the band Sons of Gorgo. Because Mydei saw those guys as his brothers.

Maybe that was the first sign that Mydei realized that he couldn’t carry her legacy alone.

Maybe he tried, and failed, and he finally got tired. Maybe he wasn’t as nonchalant as he let on. Maybe he saw the critics and felt even more guilty that no matter how hard he tried, he could never be her.

And maybe, with the praise and good reviews from the campaign about Robin’s role in reviving Queen Gorgo’s spirit, Mydei was glad to finally find someone to properly carry on his mom’s legacy without being thoroughly lost in that identity.

That Gorgo boy finally did something good, that taxi driver told him. And he was a huge Gorgo fan.

Maybe Mydei felt that, too. That he was finally doing good. Doing the right thing for her.

Phainon dragged a hand to his face.

Oh, Kephale.

He was so, so stupid.

His phone almost ran out of battery, but his eyes caught sight of one last thumbnail showing Mydei and Gorgo’s image, edited to be side by side despite the photo being taken in a different era. It was a clip from Praho Winfree Show, and the thumbnail was titled "Mydeimos Gorgo Reacts to Queen Gorgo Pregnancy Interview."

Phainon pressed play.

The video started with the old clip of Gregoria Gorgo's interview with Praho, when she was definitely pregnant with Mydei. The clip was a bit blurry, but it was still of good quality.

“One question, Gregoria,” Praho said. “If your child doesn’t have an interest in music, if this child decides to pursue something else, what will you do?”

“Then to hell with music, Winfree,” Gorgo cackled. The audience in the studio laughed along with her. “My baby can be whatever he wants. I’ll support him. This child is my prince, he’ll be king, and kings don’t bow to Queen Mother, am I right, people?”

The camera went back to Mydei when the same interviewer, now almost a decade older than when she interviewed Gregoria, asked. “So if not music, what are you going to pursue, Mydei?”

Mydei paused, thinking for a bit, before shrugging. “I can’t really imagine doing anything else. Music’s always been important to me — just like it was for Mom, Mrs. Winfree. But maybe…” he paused again. There was a slight tug on his lips. “Maybe a chef? I know this one guy who’s absolutely sucked at cooking. He survived solely on a goat diet, only salads and greens, so I’ve been trying to help and… I think I like that feeling, you know? seeing people eat the food you cook, it’s kinda the same as seeing people listening to your music.”

Phainon could feel himself smiling. He didn’t remember ever watching this interview before, but he remembered that Mydei’s bandmates had called him GOATnon for a short while after, for reasons he was still confused about. He rewinded the video and stared at Mydei’s expression when talking about Phainon in the interview, glowing, alive, free.

Phainon closed his eyes.

Oh, sweet, sweet Kephale.

He really, really should talk to Mydei.

Phainon opened Mydei's chat room, pinned to the top, but had been silent for three long weeks. He tried to type in something: Hello, Hey, I’m sorry, we should talk, are you well? But nothing felt right.

No, stop.

Phainon had to stop thinking about what felt right. He had to start thinking about the truth.

Talk about his truth.

You ‘Dei, hi. I know you’re on tour, and I understand if it takes some time, but I'd still like to talk to you if you have a moment. I mean, I could type it here, but I need to talk to you. In person. Through call. I need to talk to you. I'll fly wherever you are if I have to.

Phainon sent the message and stared at his phone like a man possessed.

He waited, and waited, and waited, but no reply ever came through.

He waited until he fell asleep, waited as his battery was full and he had to leave to his layover hotel, waited as he stayed over the three-day layover, and glanced at his phone before he boarded the plane back for the ultra-long flight back to Okhema.

Still, no reply.

None.

Phainon tried to leave another message. He typed, and deleted, and typed again, and deleted…

And decided that maybe it’s done.

Maybe Mydei truly hated him and didn’t want to have anything to do with him anymore.

So Phainon boarded the plane, counting the 17-hour flight by the second, wondering if, in one of those passing seconds, Mydei had replied to his message.

But as he arrived at Okhema, he saw that nothing.

His chat remained the last in their window.

Phainon swallowed the lump in his throat and decided to get off the aircraft. He still didn’t dare to go home, so going to HQ would be his best bet.

When he arrived there, however, Eleanor greeted him with a smile. She passed a neat envelope to Phainon with such a smug face that it made Phainon suspicious. He opened the envelope, and when he saw the words written in the paper tucked inside it, Phainon’s eyes shot up so fast he almost had whiplash.

“No,” he said.

“Yes, Captain. I did remind you that your hours in the sim program would be counted to your working hours,” she said. “You’ve exceeded your working hours. Any more hours in this building, and you risk getting us fined and losing your license. Now we wouldn’t want it, don’t we?”

Of course, he didn’t want that. Phainon gritted his teeth.

Ten days off.

What was he going to do in ten days? Where was he supposed to go in ten fucking days? He gritted his teeth, opening his mouth to argue again. But Eleanor shook her head, looking sympathetic.

“Maybe you should go home, Captain,” she said, patting Phainon’s shoulders before turning to leave. “You look like you really need a time-out with your loved ones. Visit your family, maybe? I’m sure they missed you.”

Phainon sighed.

Family.

He thought about that dream about Concorde and wheat fields, about a lonely night in Styxia, about Cyrene, and about the facts about Mydei that he had just discovered, and thought that maybe Eleanor was right.

Maybe he should go home.

But before he went back to his apartment in the heart of Okhema City, he had to make a detour to his parents’ home.

To Aedes Elysiae.

Chapter End Notes

yes, I know, I'm sorry! The happier part is in the next chapter! :D

chapters.title: Chapter 7: Paradise
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Phainon come home, and find his paradise again.

Chapter Notes

This is the final part of the two-parts last chapter before the epilogue of the story! To avoid confusion, if the last part you read was mydei and phainon breaking up, then you wanna see chapter 6 first.

Sorry I have to split it in two! It's quite a long chapter >.<

Phainon didn’t want to sit another hour in an aircraft, so he took the overnight bus to Aedes Elysiae, hoping to fall asleep in their sleeping pod. He needed a break from his own mind, and waking up refreshed sounded really nice.

But he was restless the entire journey, not getting a wink of sleep.

He tossed around in the cramped pod, only to give up halfway, and decided to stare at the dark blur outside his window, replaying the scenes from the TabTube, thinking about Mydei, about their fight, about Aventurine’s words, about everything and nothing, all while still holding his phone, waiting for a message he knew wouldn’t come.

Too late.

He was far too late.

He probably hurt Mydei too much, beyond forgiveness. After all, Aventurine said that Mydei was trying his best to keep this relationship with Phainon. He tried, fighting the battle alone while Phainon and his stupid low self-esteem decided that he was not good enough for Mydei.

Stupid, stupid Phainon.

He savored the pain by scrolling through their old chats, the better time before they fell apart. The selfies, the random pictures, the teases and jokes… Phainon frowned at his own cold replies after that Owlbert interview, the poor facade he put that he realized now wouldn’t fool Mydei.

Well, he deserved every bit of pain he was experiencing now.

If only he hadn’t run out of tears, Phainon was sure that he would cry again now.

But he was hollowed out, and he didn’t know if he could even feel something with his exhaustion.

When the bus finally entered Aedes Elysiae, dawn only began to rise from the horizon, washing the wheat field with golden color. It was beautiful, familiar, and Phainon let out a relieved sigh before he could even think of anything else. The view lightened the weight in Phainon’s chest, and he was so, so glad that Eleanor forced him to rest and visit his family.

Maybe this was what he needed.

He strolled slowly, enjoying the view while walking towards his parents’ home. There were so many sounds he missed: the bugs, the gentle breeze waving the leaves, the sound of his suitcase being dragged along the rocky road, and the sound of a morning bird chirping.

It all felt nice, though it didn’t soothe the sting of the silence of his phone in the back pocket.

His house was just like the last time Phainon left it, washed by the gold from the rising sun. It looked too warm, too quiet, and as Phainon arrived on the porch, he could hear the sounds of activity inside; the people he loved were starting their day.

He closed his eyes and knocked on the door of his parents’ home twice.

There was a muffled wait for a minute from the other side of the door, and in the next five seconds, Phainon was face-to-face with Audata, his mom.

Her smile faltered when she saw Phainon, and she shifted into mild surprise.

“Phainon?” she blinked. Phainon could see questions flicker in her eyes, but then, the first thing she asked was, “Are you okay?”

His automated answer was already in his tongue. Yes, I’m fine. Sorry, I didn’t call. But he couldn’t say them. He couldn’t speak those answers, because he knew it was a lie.

He couldn’t lie to his mother.

As if knowing Phainon’s turmoil, Audata opened her arms, inviting him for a hug.

Phainon rushed into her arms, and suddenly, he wasn’t feeling hollowed out anymore.

Emotions filled his chest like a flood, and then he cried again.

A silent sob at first, but as his mom hugged him tighter, as she soothed his back with circular motion, Phainon sobbed harder, inviting rushing footsteps from the kitchen; his father and Cyrene joined them at the door, worriedly asking what happened, why Phai was here, and then, the questions subsided, and he received more touches instead—Cyrene’s hand on his own, and his father’s pat on the back of his head.
